newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: FEATURE - Zimbabwe government to review ailing health system.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Zimbabwe government to review ailing health system.

text.p: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe is to set up a commission to review the country's public health system now tottering under crippling debts and drug and staff shortages.
Mugabe's recent announcement followed mounting complaints from the public, including many members of his ruling ZANU-PF party, about worsening standards in state health services.
"We are trying to see what it is we are doing right and what it is we are doing wrong," Mugabe told a group of Zimbabweans during a visit to New York. He gave no time frame for the review.
Mugabe has often cited advances in the public health sector, particularly in the provision of primary health care, as one of the main success stories of his 17 years in power.

But over the past year, mounting debts at state hospitals, perennial drug shortages and a series of crippling strikes by disaffected doctors and nurses have chipped away at that success and pointed to an ailing public health sector.

Figures on hospital debts are unavailable, but last year the government had to bail them out with extra cash allocations after their major suppliers suspended deliveries of food and drugs due to non-payment.
STAFF HAEMORRHAGE TO GREENER PASTURES
The hospitals have also seen a haemorrhage of skilled staff, with officials estimating that they are losing an average 30 professional workers a month to private clinics and surgeries.
In most cases, the departing staff cite poor salaries and working conditions.
These concerns prompted nurses and junior doctors to go on strike over three successive months, leading the public health sector to the brink of collapse.

"I'm just waiting to complete my compulsory housemanship and I'm off to South Africa where I think my services will be appreciated and where conditions seem better," said a junior doctor at the country's second largest hospital, Parirenyatwa.
"Standards have gone down in our hospitals and the government doesn't seem to care about doing anything about it.
"Low salaries are not the only concern. Working conditions have worsened with shortages of equipment and essential druges adding to the frustration," he said.
"Sometimes we have to improvise, using the wrong equipment for an operation and prescribing drugs which are not available in the hospital," added the doctor, who askeds not to be named.
Harare resident Helen Ngobe said she recently joined a medical aid scheme which she is struggling financially to keep up.
"I want to be able to afford to go to private clinics because I cannot stand going to government hospitals any more.
"I spent a month at Harare (state) hospital and I don't want to go through that experience again," she said.

"When I was admitted, I spent three nights lying on a mattress on the floor in a crowded ward with a sheet and one thin blanket. When I asked for another blanket because I was feeling cold the nurse told me there was a shortage of blankets so they were rationing them."
MINISTRY UNDER PRESSURE TO RECOVER DEBTS
Health experts say poor funding and misuse of available resources lie at the heart of most of the problems.
Health and Child Welfare Minister Timothy Stamps blames the World Bank for pressing the government to cut spending on social services to contain a burgeoning budget deficit.

But the country's state treasury, faced with dwindling cash in the national coffers, places part of the blame on Stamps' ministry, accusing it of mismangement, bad accounting and lax cost-recovery measures.
Stamps, whose ministry gets one of the largest shares of the national budget, has said he is under intense pressure from the auditor and comptroller-general to recover money owed to the hopsitals.
He said Parirenyatwa hospital was owed millions of dollars in unpaid fees over four years.
A substantial amount of that debt was owed by the cash-strapped government, which has failed to pay for patients covered by a social fund.
Health experts say the planned review commission should look at all these ills -- particularly sustainable financing of the sector.

"A commission is necessary, if it's going to look at the financing of the health system in this country in a sustainable manner, if it's going to look at cost-recovery issues, the quality of health care...if it's going to look at all the health problems," National Drugs and Therapist Advisory Committee chairman Norman Nyazema told Reuters.
